newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Fiat chief Romiti set for appeal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Fiat chief Romiti set for appeal.

text.p: Fiat chairman Cesare Romiti on Thursday was set to appeal against a 18-month jail sentence for false accounting at Italy's largest private industrial giant, while ex-head Gianni Agnelli stood by his old right-hand man.

The sentence was effectively suspended until the lengthy Italian judicial process is completed and Romiti may never serve the jail term, but he is Italy's most prominent business figure convicted since Italy's anti-corruption drive started in 1992.
Romiti was sentenced late Wednesday in a Turin court along with former finance director Francesco Paolo Mattiolo, who received a suspended sentence of 16 months on similar charges.

The presiding judge Francesco Saluzzo also asked for documentary evidence to be given to the state prosecutor to see if Agnelli and other members of Fiat's executive committee were guilty of any wrongdoing.

Agnelli who stepped down in March 1996 after 30 years at the helm of Fiat to become its honourary president and had worked closed with Romiti since the mid-1970s, expressed his full support for both Romiti and Mattioli.

"I believe the work of Cesare Romiti and Francesco Paolo Mattiolo, in many years of superb collaboration, has always been correct. I therefore would like to confirm my confidence in their innocence, and I believe that this will be proved in the appeal courts," Agnelli said.
However, the sentence is a severe embarrassment for Fiat and the Agnellis, with the Agnelli family holding companies IFI and IFIL holding around 32 percent of the shares of Fiat.

Fiat and the Agnelli family have been inextricably linked since Gianni Agnelli's grandfather founded the company in 1899. And when Romiti is scheduled to step down, at 75 in June 1998, many expect another Agnelli, Gianni's nephew Giovanni aged 32, to take over at the helm.

The Turin trial which started in January saw the two top executives accused of falsifying accounts to divert more than 30 billion lire ($17.6 million) in overseas accounts from the 1980s to make payments to political parties and top Fiat managers abroad.
In a further move on Thursday, the Rome state prosecutor's office requested that both Romiti and Mattioli stand trial on separate corruption charges.

According to the formal request by magistrate Francesco Misiani, Fiat allegely paid bribes between 1983 and 1992 to the then powerful Christian Democrat and Socialist parties, totalling 300 billion lire, in order to obtain contracts for construction work on Rome's underground metropolitan railway.

Many analysts were unruffled by the sentences and suggested that the appeal process was unlikely to be completed by the time Romiti steps down next June, and suggested that he may never see jail as sentences under two years for people with no previous convictions are usually suspended.

Fiat shares reacted calmly, being marked down largely in line with the lower overall stock market. Some suggested a bit of weakness may have been added by March new car registrations data out on Thursday.
These figures showed Fiat's domestic market share slipping, indicating the Turin auto maker be struggling to keep pace with a sharply rising Italian car market.
At 1212 GMT, Fiat shares were off 0.66 percent at 5,455 lire with the Milan stock market's MIB30 all-share index down 0.42 percent.
